metadata.title: On the Unique Crossing Conjecture of Diaconis and Perlman on Convolutions of Gamma Random Variables

nodes.name: Distribution function F_theta of a weighted sum of iid gammas
nodes.statement: Let $X_1,\ldots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed (iid) gamma($\alpha, 1$) random variables and denote the distribution function for $\sum_{i=1}^n \theta_i X_i$ by $F_\theta$ where $\theta \equiv (\theta_1,\ldots, \theta_n)$ is a nonnegative weight vector.
nodes.statement_short: $F_\theta$ is the cdf of $\sum_i \theta_i X_i$ with $X_i$ iid gamma($\alpha,1$) and nonnegative weights $\theta$.

nodes.name: Unique crossing conjecture (UCC) of Diaconis and Perlman
nodes.statement: If $\eta\prec \theta$ (Marshall, Olkin and Arnold 2009), but $\theta$ is not a permutation of $\eta$, then $F_\eta(x) -F_\theta(x)$ changes signs exactly once, from $-$ to $+$, as $x$ increases from $0$ to $\infty$.
assumptions: $\eta\prec \theta$
$\theta$ is not a permutation of $\eta$
conclusions: $F_\eta(x) -F_\theta(x)$ changes signs exactly once, from $-$ to $+$, as $x$ increases from $0$ to $\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\eta$ is majorized by $\theta$ (not a permutation), $F_\eta-F_\theta$ changes sign exactly once, from $-$ to $+$.
nodes.label: conj1

nodes.name: Diaconis-Perlman special cases of the UCC
nodes.statement: Disconis and Perlman verified the UCC in the following cases: (a) $n=2$; (b) $n=3$ and $\alpha=1$; (c) $n\geq 3,\ \alpha\geq 1$ and $\theta$ and $\eta$ differ in only two components; (d) $n\geq 3$ and components of $\eta$ are equal.
conclusions: (a) $n=2$; (b) $n=3$ and $\alpha=1$; (c) $n\geq 3,\ \alpha\geq 1$ and $\theta$ and $\eta$ differ in only two components; (d) $n\geq 3$ and components of $\eta$ are equal.
nodes.statement_short: The UCC holds for $n=2$; for $n=3,\alpha=1$; for $\alpha\ge1$ when the weights differ in two components; and when $\eta$ has equal components.

nodes.name: Unique crossing under a one-sign-change configuration ($\alpha\ge 1$)
nodes.statement: Suppose $\alpha \geq 1$. Suppose $0<\theta_1\leq \cdots \leq \theta_n$ and $\eta_1\leq \cdots \leq \eta_n$ and (a) there exists $2\leq k\leq n$ such that $\theta_i<\eta_i$ for $i< k$ and $\theta_i > \eta_i$ for $i\geq k$; (b) $\prod_{i=1}^n \eta_i > \prod_{i=1}^n \theta_i$. Then there exists $x_0\in (0, \infty)$ such that $F_\eta(x) < F_\theta(x)$ for $x\in (0, x_0)$ and the inequality is reversed for $x> x_0$.
assumptions: $\alpha \geq 1$
$0<\theta_1\leq \cdots \leq \theta_n$ and $\eta_1\leq \cdots \leq \eta_n$
(a) there exists $2\leq k\leq n$ such that $\theta_i<\eta_i$ for $i< k$ and $\theta_i > \eta_i$ for $i\geq k$
(b) $\prod_{i=1}^n \eta_i > \prod_{i=1}^n \theta_i$
conclusions: there exists $x_0\in (0, \infty)$ such that $F_\eta(x) < F_\theta(x)$ for $x\in (0, x_0)$ and the inequality is reversed for $x> x_0$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\alpha\ge1$, if $\theta_i-\eta_i$ changes sign once (from $-$ to $+$) and $\prod\eta_i>\prod\theta_i$, then $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once from below.
nodes.label: thm1

nodes.name: UCC when the weight vectors differ in at most three components
nodes.statement: The UCC is valid if $n\geq 3,\ \alpha\geq 1$ and the weight vectors differ in at most three components.
assumptions: $n\geq 3,\ \alpha\geq 1$ and the weight vectors differ in at most three components
conclusions: The UCC is valid
nodes.label: coro0

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: When $n=3$, conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm1} can be written as $\eta_{(1)} > \theta_{(1)},\ \eta_{(3)} < \theta_{(3)}$ and $\theta_1\theta_2\theta_3 <\eta_1\eta_2\eta_3$. It is easy to verify that if $\eta\prec \theta$ then these conditions are satisfied (if any $\eta_i=\theta_j$ then the problem reduces to the $n=2$ case). As noted by Diaconis and Perlman, when $\alpha\geq 1$, one may extend the validity of the UCC for $n=3$ to $n\geq 3$ provided that the weight vectors differ in at most three components.
nodes.statement_short: Check that for $n=3$ majorization implies the conditions of Theorem 1, then extend to $n\ge3$ via Diaconis-Perlman's observation.

nodes.name: Remark 1: relaxing the conditions of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 1.} The conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm1} may be relaxed to allow $\theta_i= \eta_i$ for some $i<n$ but we cannot relax the assumption $\theta_n > \eta_n$, which ensures that $F_\eta(x) > F_\theta(x)$ for large enough $x$. For example, letting $n=3,\, \alpha=1$, $\theta=(1, 6, 10)$ and $\eta = (4, 5, 10)$ we can directly check that $F_\theta\leq_{\rm st} F_\eta$ and there is no crossing. When $\theta_n = \eta_n$, deciding whether there is one crossing or no crossing requires additional analysis.
nodes.statement_short: Ties $\theta_i=\eta_i$ for $i<n$ are allowed but $\theta_n>\eta_n$ is needed; example $\theta=(1,6,10)$, $\eta=(4,5,10)$ has no crossing.

nodes.name: Log-majorization implies stochastic dominance (Yu 2011)
nodes.statement: For $n \geq 2$ and $\alpha >0$, if $\log \eta \prec \log \theta$ then $F_\eta(x)\geq F_\theta(x)$ for all $x\in (0, \infty)$. That is, $F_\eta$ is stochastically dominated by $F_\theta$.
assumptions: $n \geq 2$ and $\alpha >0$
$\log \eta \prec \log \theta$
conclusions: $F_\eta(x)\geq F_\theta(x)$ for all $x\in (0, \infty)$
nodes.label: lem1

nodes.name: Unique crossing criterion for $n=2$
nodes.statement: Suppose $n=2$. Then $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once, and from below, as $x$ increases from $0$ to $\infty$ if and only if $\theta_1 \theta_2 < \eta_1 \eta_2$ and $\max(\theta_1, \theta_2) > \max(\eta_1, \eta_2)$.
assumptions: Suppose $n=2$
conclusions: $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once, and from below, as $x$ increases from $0$ to $\infty$ if and only if $\theta_1 \theta_2 < \eta_1 \eta_2$ and $\max(\theta_1, \theta_2) > \max(\eta_1, \eta_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: For $n=2$, $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once from below iff $\theta_1\theta_2<\eta_1\eta_2$ and $\max\theta>\max\eta$.
nodes.label: prop1

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Let us assume $\theta_1 \leq \theta_2$ and $\eta_1 \leq \eta_2$ without loss of generality. {\bf Necessity.} Suppose $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once from below. Then $F_\eta(x) -F_\theta(x)$ is negative for sufficiently small $x>0$ and is positive for sufficiently large $x$. But $$\frac{1 - F_\theta(x)}{1 - F_\eta(x)} \leq \frac{\Pr(\theta_2 (X_1+X_2) > x)}{\Pr(\eta_2 X_2 > x)}.$$ The latter ratio is asymptotic to $g_{2\alpha}(x/\theta_2)/ g_\alpha(x/\eta_2)$ as $x\to \infty$ where $g_\alpha(t) \equiv t^{\alpha -1} e^{-t} /\Gamma(\alpha)$. It is clear that if $\theta_2 < \eta_2$ then $(1 - F_\theta(x))/(1 - F_\eta(x))\to 0$ as $x\to\infty$ and hence we must have $\theta_2> \eta_2$. (It is easy to dismiss the boundary case $\theta_2 = \eta_2$.) On the other hand, $$\lim_{x\downarrow 0} \frac{F_\theta(x)}{F_\eta(x)} = \lim_{x\downarrow 0} \frac{ f_\theta(x) }{f_\eta(x)} = \left(\frac{\theta_1\theta_2}{\eta_1\eta_2}\right)^{-\alpha},$$ see, for example, Yu (2009), Equation (13). Hence we must have $\theta_1\theta_2 \leq \eta_1\eta_2$. To rule out the boundary case, note that if $\theta_1\theta_2 = \eta_1\eta_2$, then $(\log\eta_1, \log\eta_2)\prec (\log \theta_1, \log \theta_2)$ and, by Lemma~\ref{lem1}, there is no crossing. {\bf Sufficiency.} Assume $\theta_1\theta_2 < \eta_1 \eta_2$ and $\theta_2 > \eta_2$. Retracing the proof of the necessity part, we can deduce that $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ at least once, from below. To show that the crossing point is unique we slightly extend the arguments of Diaconis and Perlman (1990). We have $$F_\theta(x) - F_\eta(x) = x u^{-2} \int_0^\infty (H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u)) g_{2\alpha}(x/u) {\rm d} u$$ where $H_\theta(u) = \Pr(\theta_1 W_1 + \theta_2 W_2 \leq u)$ and $W_1$ is a beta($\alpha, \alpha$) random variable with $W_1 = 1-W_2 = X_1/(X_1 + X_2).$ The kernel $g_{2\alpha}(x/u)$ is strictly totally positive (STP) for $(x, u) \in (0, \infty)^2$. The claim would follow from variation-diminishing properties of STP kernels if we can show that $H_\theta(u) -H_\eta(u)$ changes signs only once, from $+$ to $-$, as u increases on $(0, \infty)$. Note that $$H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u) =B\left(\frac{\eta_2 - u}{\eta_2 -\eta_1}\right) - B\left(\frac{\theta_2 -u}{\theta_2 -\theta_1}\right)$$ where $B(\cdot)$ denotes the beta($\alpha, \alpha$) distribution function. Let $$u^* = \frac{\theta_2 \eta_1 - \eta_2 \theta_1}{\theta_2 -\theta_1 -\eta_2 +\eta_1}.$$ Under the assumptions we have $\theta_1< \eta_1 \leq \eta_2 <\theta_2$. It follows that $\eta_1 \leq u^* \leq \eta_2 $ and $$ H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u) \begin{cases} > 0 & {\rm if}\ \theta_1 < u < u^*,\\ < 0 & {\rm if}\ u^* < u < \theta_2,\\ =0 & {\rm otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ That is, $H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u)$ has only one sign change at $u^*$, as needed.
nodes.statement_short: Necessity from tail asymptotics and the small-$x$ density ratio; sufficiency via a mixture representation with an STP kernel and variation diminishing.

nodes.name: Remark 2: relation to the star order results of Kochar and Xu
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 2.} This Proposition is closely related to Theorem~3.6 of Kochar and Xu (2011) and Proposition~3.1 of Kochar and Xu (2012) who compare $F_\theta$ and $F_\eta$ according to the {\it star order} (Shaked and Shanthikumar, 2007). $F_\eta \leq_{*} F_\theta$ means $F_\eta(x)$ crosses $F_\theta(cx)$ at most once, and always from below, for all $c>0$. Proposition~\ref{prop1} can be used to recover a special case of Proposition~3.1 of Kochar and Xu (2012).
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 1 relates to Kochar-Xu star-order comparisons and recovers a special case of their Proposition 3.1.

nodes.name: Star order
nodes.statement: $F_\eta \leq_{*} F_\theta$ means $F_\eta(x)$ crosses $F_\theta(cx)$ at most once, and always from below, for all $c>0$.
differentia: $F_\eta(x)$ crosses $F_\theta(cx)$ at most once, and always from below, for all $c>0$

nodes.name: Star-order comparison for $n=2$
nodes.statement: If $\theta_2>\theta_1,\ \eta_2>\eta_1$ and $\theta_2/\theta_1 > \eta_2/\eta_1$ then $F_\eta \leq_* F_\theta$.
assumptions: $\theta_2>\theta_1,\ \eta_2>\eta_1$ and $\theta_2/\theta_1 > \eta_2/\eta_1$
conclusions: $F_\eta \leq_* F_\theta$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2
nodes.statement: In the stated parameter configuration one can show that, for every $c>0$, either $\theta$ and $c\eta$ satisfy the necessary conditions of Proposition~\ref{prop1} and $F_\theta$ and $F_{c\eta} $ cross exactly once, or they are ordered by the usual stochastic order, and there is no crossing. In other words, $F_\eta \leq_* F_\theta$.
nodes.statement_short: For each scale $c$, either Proposition 1 gives one crossing of $F_\theta$ and $F_{c\eta}$ or they are stochastically ordered.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
We use induction on $n$. The case of $n=2$ is given by Proposition~ef{prop1}. Suppose $n\geq 3$. The following argument works for $k<n$, and can be modified (with a different definition of $	au$) to handle the $k=n$ case. Let us consider $	au \equiv (	heta_1, \ldots, 	heta_{k-2}, \delta, \eta_{k}, 	heta_{k+1}, \ldots, 	heta_n),$ where $$\delta_*\equiv  rac{	heta_{k-1}	heta_{k}}{\eta_{k}}\leq \delta\leq \min\left(	heta_{k},\, \prod_{i
eq k} \eta_i/\prod_{i
eq k-1, k} 	heta_iight)\equiv \delta^*.$$ It is easy to see that $\delta_*<\delta^*$, and for $\delta\in (\delta_*, \delta^*)$ we have $\delta > 	heta_{k-1}$ and $\prod_{i=1}^n \eta_i > \prod_{i=1}^n 	au_i > \prod_{i=1}^n 	heta_i$. Also, $	au_i <\eta_i$ for $i< k-1$ and $	au_i >\eta_i$ for $i\geq k+1$ (including $i=n$ since $k<n$). Hence the sequence $	au_{(i)} - \eta_i,\ i=1,\ldots, n$, has exactly one sign change, whether $\delta > \eta_{k-1}$ or not. (In the special case $k=2$ we have $\delta < \eta_1$.) Here we use $	au_{(i)}$ rather than $	au_i$ to account for possible switching between $\eta_{k-1}$ and $\delta$ when we rearrange $	au$. As $	au$ and $	heta$ differ in only two components, and $	au$ and $\eta$ have at least one ($\eta_k$) in common, by the induction hypothesis, $F_	au$ crosses $F_	heta$ at most once, from below (say at $x_*$) and $F_\eta$ crosses $F_	au$ at most once, from below (say at $x^*$). When $\alpha \geq 1$ the gamma density is log-concave, which ensures that adding identical components does not create multiple crossings. It is possible that the original single crossing is annihilated. If $\delta$ is large then $F_	au$ could stay entirely below $F_	heta$ (effectively $x_*=\infty$). It is not possible, however, for $F_\eta$ to stay entirely below $F_	au$, because $	au_n>\eta_n$. Note that $F_	au$ stochastically increases in $\delta$, which implies that $x_*$ increases while $x^*$ decreases in $\delta$. This monotonicity can then be used to show that the crossing points (as long as they are finite) are continuous functions of $\delta$. Specifically, fix $\delta_0\in (\delta_*, \delta^*)$ such that $x_*(\delta_0)$ is finite. Then, by the continuity of $F_	heta$ and $F_	au$, and the monotonicity of $x_*$, we have $$F_	heta(x_*(\delta_0 +)) = \lim_{\delta \downarrow \delta_0} F_	heta(x_*(\delta)) = \lim_{\delta \downarrow \delta_0} F_	au (x_*(\delta)) = F_{	au(\delta_0)}(x_*(\delta_0 + )). $$ That is, $F_	heta$ and $F_{	au(\delta_0)}$ crosses at $x_*(\delta_0 +)$. By uniqueness of the crossing point we have $x_*(\delta_0) = x_*(\delta_0 +)$, and similarly $x_*(\delta_0) = x_*(\delta_0 -)$, showing that $x_*$ is continuous. At $\delta = \delta_*$, we have $F_	au\leq_{m st} F_	heta$ by Lemma~ef{lem1}. So there is no crossing between $F_	au$ and $F_	heta$. That is, $x_*\downarrow 0$ as $\delta\downarrow \delta_*$ and $\lim_{\delta\downarrow \delta_*} x^* >0$. At $\delta = 	heta_k$ we have $F_	au\geq_{m st} F_	heta$. Thus $x_*\uparrow \infty$ as $\delta\uparrow 	heta_k$ if $\delta^*=	heta_k$. The other possibility is $\delta^* = \prod_{i
eq k} \eta_i/\prod_{i
eq k, k-1} 	heta_i$. In this case, at $\delta=\delta^*$ we have $F_	au\geq_{m st} F_\eta$ again by Lemma~ef{lem1}, because $\log\eta\prec \log	au$. Indeed, because $\log(\eta_i/	au_i)$ changes signs only once (after $	au$ is arranged in increasing order), $\sum_{i=1}^l \log(\eta_i/	au_i)$ first increases, and then decreases. At $l=1$ we have $\eta_1>	au_1$. At $l=n$ we have $\sum_{i=1}^n \log(\eta_i/ 	au_i) = 0$. Thus $\sum_{i=1}^l \log(\eta_i/ 	au_i) \geq 0$ for all $l=1,\ldots, n$, that is, $\log\eta\prec\log	au$. It follows that $x^*\downarrow 0$ as $\delta\uparrow \delta^*$. Regardless of whether $\delta^*=	heta_k$, we have $x_*< x^*$ as $\delta	o \delta_*$ and $x_* > x^*$ as $\delta	o \delta^*$. By continuity, there exists some $\delta$ such that $x_*=x^*$ and  egin{align*} F_	heta(x) &> F_	au(x)> F_\eta(x),\quad 0<x<x^*;\ F_	heta(x) &< F_	au(x)< F_\eta(x),\quad x^*<x<\infty. \end{align*} It follows that $F_\eta$ crosses $F_	heta$ exactly once, from below.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ via an intermediate vector $\tau(\delta)$ that crosses both $F_\theta$ and $F_\eta$ once. Continuity of the two crossing points in $\delta$ yields a $\delta$ where they coincide.

nodes.name: Counterexamples extend to $n>3$
nodes.statement: Note that counterexamples for $n>3$ can be generated from a counterexample for $n=3$ by appending small enough components to the weight vectors.
conclusions: Note that counterexamples for $n>3$ can be generated from a counterexample for $n=3$ by appending small enough components to the weight vectors.

nodes.name: Outline of the counterexample construction
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm2} is derived through a perturbation analysis rather than extensive numerical calculations. Our counterexamples have the feature that $\theta_1 \approx \theta_2 \ll \theta_3$, and $\eta$ is a small perturbation of $\theta$ which changes all three components. We show that for a suitable choice of such $\theta$ and $\eta$, there exists a point at which $F_\eta(x)$ crosses $F_\theta(x)$ from above. Since $F_\eta(x)$ has to cross $F_\theta(x)$ from below for sufficiently small $x> 0$ and for sufficiently large $x$, it follows that there are at least three crossing points. The rest of this section makes this precise.
nodes.statement_short: Perturbation analysis with $\theta_1\approx\theta_2\ll\theta_3$ produces a crossing from above, hence at least three crossings.

nodes.name: Failure of the UCC for $\alpha<1$
nodes.statement: For every $0<\alpha < 1$ there exist positive vectors $\theta$ and $\eta$ with $n=3$ such that $\eta\prec \theta$ and $F_\eta(x) -F_\theta(x)$ changes signs at least three times as $x$ increases from $0$ to $\infty$.
assumptions: every $0<\alpha < 1$
conclusions: there exist positive vectors $\theta$ and $\eta$ with $n=3$ such that $\eta\prec \theta$ and $F_\eta(x) -F_\theta(x)$ changes signs at least three times as $x$ increases from $0$ to $\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: For each $\alpha\in(0,1)$ there are $\eta\prec\theta$ with $n=3$ such that $F_\eta-F_\theta$ changes sign at least three times.
nodes.label: thm2

nodes.name: Derivative of a gamma convolution cdf under a two-weight transfer
nodes.statement: Suppose $X_i$ and $Z_i,\ i=1,2$ are independent random variables with $X_i\sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha, 1)$ and $Z_i\sim {\rm expo}(1),\ i =1, 2$, and, independently, $G$ is a weighted sum of iid gamma variates. Fix $\theta_i^*>0,\ i=1,2$ and let $\theta_1 = \theta_1^* -\delta$ and $\theta_2 = \theta_2^* +\delta$. Then $$\frac{\partial}{\partial \delta} \Pr(\theta_1 X_1 + \theta_2 X_2 + G\leq x) = \alpha (\theta_2 -\theta_1) \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} \Pr(\theta_1(X_1 + Z_1) + \theta_2 (X_2 + Z_2) + G\leq x). $$
nodes.origin_citation: Rinott, Scarsini and Yu 2012, Lemma 1 (modified); Szekely and Bakirov 2003
assumptions: Suppose $X_i$ and $Z_i,\ i=1,2$ are independent random variables with $X_i\sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha, 1)$ and $Z_i\sim {\rm expo}(1),\ i =1, 2$, and, independently, $G$ is a weighted sum of iid gamma variates.
Fix $\theta_i^*>0,\ i=1,2$ and let $\theta_1 = \theta_1^* -\delta$ and $\theta_2 = \theta_2^* +\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Moving mass $\delta$ between two weights changes the cdf at rate $\alpha(\theta_2-\theta_1)$ times a second $x$-derivative of an augmented cdf.
nodes.label: lem2

nodes.name: Gamma density $g_\alpha$
nodes.statement: We also need a result concerning mixtures of gamma densities ($g_\alpha(t)\equiv t^{\alpha -1} e^{-t}/\Gamma(\alpha)$).

nodes.name: Bimodality of gamma mixtures iff $\alpha<1$
nodes.statement: If $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ then there exists $\lambda \in (0, \infty)$ such that the mixture density $(\lambda g_{1+\alpha}(x) + g_{\alpha}(x))/(1+\lambda)$ is bimodal. There exists no such $\lambda$ if $\alpha \geq 1$.
assumptions: $\alpha \in (0, 1)$
conclusions: there exists $\lambda \in (0, \infty)$ such that the mixture density $(\lambda g_{1+\alpha}(x) + g_{\alpha}(x))/(1+\lambda)$ is bimodal.
There exists no such $\lambda$ if $\alpha \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: The mixture of $g_{1+\alpha}$ and $g_\alpha$ can be bimodal exactly when $\alpha<1$.
nodes.label: lem3

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: For any $x_0\in (0, \alpha)$ one may set $\lambda \equiv \lambda(x_0)= - g'_{\alpha}(x_0) / g'_{1+\alpha}(x_0)$ and obtain a function $s(x)\equiv \lambda g_{1+\alpha}(x) + g_{\alpha}(x)$ such that $s'(x_0) = 0$. Note that since $x_0$ is between the modes of $g_{1+\alpha}$ and $g_{\alpha}$ we necessarily have $\lambda>0$. We show that $\alpha\in (0, 1)$ is equivalent to the existence of some $x_0$ such that $s''(x_0)>0$, which indicates a local minimum. By direct calculation we get $$s''(x_0) = \lambda g''_{1+\alpha}(x_0) + g''_{\alpha}(x_0) = -\lambda'(x_0) g'_{1+\alpha}(x_0)$$ with $$ \lambda'(x_0) =\frac{\alpha (x_0^2 + 2(1-\alpha )x_0 - \alpha(1-\alpha))}{(\alpha x_0- x_0^2)^2}. $$ Thus $s''(x_0)$ has the opposite sign of $x_0^2 + 2(1-\alpha )x_0 - \alpha(1-\alpha)$. If $\alpha<1$ then this quadratic is negative for sufficiently small $x_0>0$; if $\alpha \geq 1$ then it is positive for all $x_0>0$. Thus a local minimum exists if and only if $\alpha\in (0, 1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\lambda$ to make $x_0$ a stationary point of the mixture and compute the sign of $s''(x_0)$ via $\lambda'(x_0)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement:
Since $\alpha\in (0, 1)$, by Lemma~ef{lem3} one can choose $\lambda>0$ such that $s(x)\equiv \lambda g_{1+\alpha}(x) + g_{\alpha}(x)$ is bimodal, with a local minimum at $x_0>0$. nodes.name: Unique crossing conjecture holds for $\alpha\ge 1$
nodes.statement: Conjecture~\ref{conj1} is valid if $\alpha \geq 1$.
assumptions: $\alpha \geq 1$
conclusions: Conjecture~\ref{conj1} is valid
nodes.label: main.thm

nodes.name: Proof roadmap for the main theorem
nodes.statement: The rest of this paper is devoted to a proof of the above result. We extend the techniques of the previous section. By analyzing the distribution function crossing patterns of gamma convolutions we reduce the problem to a particular configuration of the weight vectors $\theta$ and $\eta$ that are sufficiently close. For this local case, relationship between crossing points to modes of a mixture of gamma convolutions is explored. We introduce a new stochastic order and derive monotonicity properties concerning densities of gamma convolutions. These tools further reduce the problem, leading to Theorem~\ref{main.thm}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a local configuration, relate crossings to modes of gamma-convolution mixtures, and use a new stochastic order.

nodes.name: Local unique crossing for a particular configuration
nodes.statement: Suppose $\alpha\geq 1$. Given an index $1<k<n-1$ let $0<\theta_1\leq \cdots \leq \theta_{k-1}<\theta_k\leq \theta_{k+1}< \theta_{k+2}\leq\cdots \leq \theta_n$ and $\delta_i>0,\ i=1,\ldots, n$, and let $\eta$ be defined as follows. $$ \eta_i = \begin{cases} &\theta_i + \delta_i,\quad i=1,\ldots, k-1;\\ & \theta_i - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \delta_j, \quad i=k;\\ & \theta_i + \sum_{j=k+2}^n \delta_j, \quad i=k+1;\\ & \theta_i -\delta_i,\quad i=k+2,\ldots, n. \end{cases} $$ Then $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once from below if $\sum_{i\neq k, k+1} \delta_i $ is small enough.
assumptions: Suppose $\alpha\geq 1$

Given an index $1<k<n-1$ let $0<\theta_1\leq \cdots \leq \theta_{k-1}<\theta_k\leq \theta_{k+1}< \theta_{k+2}\leq\cdots \leq \theta_n$ and $\delta_i>0,\ i=1,\ldots, n$, and let $\eta$ be defined as follows. $$ \eta_i = \begin{cases} &\theta_i + \delta_i,\quad i=1,\ldots, k-1;\\ & \theta_i - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \delta_j, \quad i=k;\\ & \theta_i + \sum_{j=k+2}^n \delta_j, \quad i=k+1;\\ & \theta_i -\delta_i,\quad i=k+2,\ldots, n. \end{cases} $$
conclusions: Then $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once from below if $\sum_{i\neq k, k+1} \delta_i $ is small enough.
nodes.statement_short: For $\alpha\ge1$ and $\eta$ a small transfer toward the middle indices $k,k+1$, $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once from below.
nodes.label: lem.loc

nodes.name: Order statistics $\theta_{(i)}$
nodes.statement: As usual we write $\theta_{(1)},\theta_{(2)},..., \theta_{(n)}$ as $\theta$ rearranged in increasing order.

nodes.name: V-majorization
nodes.statement: We say a real vector $\theta$ {\it V-majorizes} $\eta$, written as $\eta\prec_{\rm V} \theta$, if there exists $\tilde{\theta}$ such that $\eta\prec \tilde{\theta}$ and indices $1\leq k_1, k_2\leq n$ such that \begin{equation} \theta_{(i)}\begin{cases} \leq &\tilde{\theta}_{(i)}\leq \eta_{(i)},\quad 1\leq i\leq k_1;\\ = & \tilde{\theta}_{(i)},\quad k_1<i<k_2;\\ \geq & \tilde{\theta}_{(i)}\geq \eta_{(i)},\quad k_2\leq i \leq n. \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\theta$ V-majorizes $\eta$ if $\theta$ arises from some $\tilde\theta\succ\eta$ by pushing its already-extreme small/large coordinates further out.

nodes.name: V-majorization coordinate conditions
nodes.statement: \theta_{(i)}\begin{cases} \leq &\tilde{\theta}_{(i)}\leq \eta_{(i)},\quad 1\leq i\leq k_1;\\ = & \tilde{\theta}_{(i)},\quad k_1<i<k_2;\\ \geq & \tilde{\theta}_{(i)}\geq \eta_{(i)},\quad k_2\leq i \leq n. \end{cases}
nodes.label: major.V

nodes.name: Properties of V-majorization
nodes.statement: Let $\eta,\, \theta$ be positive vectors such that $\eta\prec_{\rm V} \theta$. (a) If $\prod_{i=1}^n (\eta_i/\theta_i) \geq 1$ then $\log \eta \prec^w \log\theta$. (b) If $\prod_{i=1}^n (\eta_i/\theta_i) \leq 1$ then $F_\eta \leq_{\rm st} F_\theta$.
assumptions: Let $\eta,\, \theta$ be positive vectors such that $\eta\prec_{\rm V} \theta$.
conclusions: (a) If $\prod_{i=1}^n (\eta_i/\theta_i) \geq 1$ then $\log \eta \prec^w \log\theta$.
(b) If $\prod_{i=1}^n (\eta_i/\theta_i) \leq 1$ then $F_\eta \leq_{\rm st} F_\theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Under V-majorization, $\prod\eta_i/\theta_i\ge1$ gives weak log-majorization and $\le1$ gives stochastic dominance.
nodes.label: prop.V

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Assume the coordinates of $\theta$ (respectively, $\eta$) are arranged in increasing order, and assume $\theta\neq \eta$. Let $\tilde{\theta}$ (also arranged in increasing order) be such that $\eta\prec \tilde{\theta}$ and (\ref{major.V}) is satisfied. Part (a). Note that $\tilde{\theta}_i \geq \theta_i$ for $1\leq i<k_2$. From $\eta\prec\tilde{\theta}$ we get $\log\eta\prec^w \log\tilde{\theta}$ and $$\prod_{i=1}^l \eta_i \geq \prod_{i=1}^l \tilde{\theta}_i \geq \prod_{i=1}^l \theta_i,\quad 1\leq l<k_2. $$ For $i\geq k_2$ we have $\eta_i \leq \theta_i$ which means $\prod_{i=1}^l (\eta_i /\theta_i)$ between $l=k_2-1$ and $l=n$ is minimized at $l=n$. Thus, to ensure $\log \eta \prec^w \log \theta$ we only need $\prod_{i=1}^n \eta_i \geq \prod_{i=1}^n \theta_i$. Part (b). We may define $$\theta^*_i \equiv \begin{cases} \theta_i & i< k_2, \\ \theta_i^{1-\lambda} \eta_i^{\lambda} & i\geq k_2; \end{cases} \quad \quad \lambda = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \log (\theta_i/\eta_i) }{\sum_{i=k_2}^n \log (\theta_i / \eta_i)}.$$ Then $\lambda\in [0, 1],\, \theta^*\leq \theta$ (coordinate-wise), and $\prod_{i=1}^n (\eta_i/\theta^*_i) = 1$. The reasoning of part (a) yields $\log\eta \prec \log \theta^*$. By Lemma~\ref{lem1}, $F_\eta\leq_{\rm st} F_{\theta^*}\leq_{\rm st} F_\theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (a) compares partial products using $\tilde\theta$; part (b) shrinks the top coordinates geometrically to equalize products and applies Lemma 1.

nodes.name: Unique crossing under V-majorization ($\alpha\ge1$)
nodes.statement: Suppose $\alpha\geq 1$, and $\eta,\, \theta$ are positive weight vectors such that $\eta \prec_{\rm V} \theta$, $\theta_{(n)}> \eta_{(n)}$ and $\prod_{i=1}^n (\eta_i/\theta_i) >1$. Then there exists $x_0\in (0, \infty)$ such that $F_\eta(x) < F_\theta(x)$ for $x\in (0, x_0)$ and $F_\eta(x) > F_\theta(x)$ for $x>x_0$.
assumptions: Suppose $\alpha\geq 1$, and $\eta,\, \theta$ are positive weight vectors such that $\eta \prec_{\rm V} \theta$, $\theta_{(n)}> \eta_{(n)}$ and $\prod_{i=1}^n (\eta_i/\theta_i) >1$
conclusions: Then there exists $x_0\in (0, \infty)$ such that $F_\eta(x) < F_\theta(x)$ for $x\in (0, x_0)$ and $F_\eta(x) > F_\theta(x)$ for $x>x_0$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\alpha\ge1$, if $\eta\prec_V\theta$, $\theta_{(n)}>\eta_{(n)}$ and $\prod\eta_i/\theta_i>1$, then $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once from below.
nodes.label: s.main

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$: build a continuum of intermediate vectors $\rho(s)$ each crossing $F_\theta$ once, using Lemma 4 locally and Theorem 1 elsewhere. A maximality argument over a parameter set $\Omega_0$ pins the crossing at $x_*$.

nodes.name: Interpolating weight vector $\tau(t_1,t_2)$
nodes.statement: \tau_i \equiv \begin{cases} \theta_i + t_1 \delta_i & i< j,\\ \theta_i - t_1 \sum_{l=1}^{j-1} \delta_l & i=j,\\ \theta_i & j<i<k;\\ \theta_i - t_2 \sum_{l=k+1}^n \delta_l & i=k,\\ \theta_i + t_2 \delta_i & i> k. \end{cases}
nodes.label: tau.def

nodes.name: Single crossing of $F_{\tau(t^*)}$ and $F_\theta$ at $x_*$
nodes.statement: F_{\tau(t^*)}(x) < F_\theta(x),\quad x\in (0, x_*);\quad F_{\tau(t^*)}(x) > F_\theta(x), \quad x> x_*.
nodes.label: t.star

nodes.name: Local unique crossing from unimodality of mixtures
nodes.statement: For a fixed positive weight vector $\theta$, let $\eta$ be defined by $\eta = \theta +\sum_{k=1}^K \tau^{(k)}$ where, associated with each $k$, we have a pair of indices $i_k\neq j_k$ and a real number $\delta_k>0$ such that $\theta_{i_k}< \theta_{j_k}$ and $$\tau^{(k)}_i = \begin{cases} \delta_k & i=i_k,\\ -\delta_k & i=j_k,\\ 0 & {\rm otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ Let $f_k(x|\delta),\ \delta\equiv (\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_K),$ denote the density of $\sum_{i=1}^n \eta_i X_i + \eta_{i_k} Z_{i_k} + \eta_{j_k} Z_{j_k}$, where $X_i\sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha, 1),\, Z_i\sim {\rm expo}(1)$ are mutually independent. Suppose, for arbitrary constants $\lambda_k\geq 0$ such that $\sum_k \lambda_k =1$, we have $\sum_k \lambda_k f_k(x|0)$ is unimodal, with a strictly negative second derivative at the mode, and no saddle points. Then for small enough $\sum_{k=1}^K \delta_k$, $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once, from below.
assumptions: For a fixed positive weight vector $\theta$, let $\eta$ be defined by $\eta = \theta +\sum_{k=1}^K \tau^{(k)}$ where, associated with each $k$, we have a pair of indices $i_k\neq j_k$ and a real number $\delta_k>0$ such that $\theta_{i_k}< \theta_{j_k}$ and $$\tau^{(k)}_i = \begin{cases} \delta_k & i=i_k,\\ -\delta_k & i=j_k,\\ 0 & {\rm otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ Let $f_k(x|\delta),\ \delta\equiv (\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_K),$ denote the density of $\sum_{i=1}^n \eta_i X_i + \eta_{i_k} Z_{i_k} + \eta_{j_k} Z_{j_k}$, where $X_i\sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha, 1),\, Z_i\sim {\rm expo}(1)$ are mutually independent.

Suppose, for arbitrary constants $\lambda_k\geq 0$ such that $\sum_k \lambda_k =1$, we have $\sum_k \lambda_k f_k(x|0)$ is unimodal, with a strictly negative second derivative at the mode, and no saddle points.
conclusions: Then for small enough $\sum_{k=1}^K \delta_k$, $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once, from below.
nodes.statement_short: If all mixtures of the augmented densities $f_k(\cdot|0)$ are strictly unimodal, then small local transfers give exactly one crossing.
nodes.label: analytic

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: Note that $\eta\prec\theta$ if $\delta$ is small enough, and hence $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ at least once, from below. By Lemma~\ref{lem2} we have $$\frac{\partial{F_{\eta}(x)}}{\partial \delta_k} = \alpha (\eta_{i_k} - \eta_{j_k}) f'_k(x| \delta),\quad k=1,\ldots, K.$$ Then, \begin{equation} F_{\eta}(x) - F_\theta(x) = \int_0^1 \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha (\theta_{i_k} - \theta_{j_k}+ 2t\delta_k) \delta_k f'_k(x|t\delta)\, {\rm d} t. \end{equation} Suppose the claim does not hold, and there exists a sequence $\eta(l)$ corresponding to $\delta(l)\equiv (\delta_{1l}, \ldots, \delta_{Kl})$ such that $\delta(l) \to 0$ and $F_{\eta(l)}(x)-F_\theta(x)=0$ has at least two roots in $x\in (0,\infty)$, for each $l=1,2,\ldots$. Denote $L(\delta) = \sum_{k=1}^K \delta_k (\theta_{i_k} - \theta_{j_k})$. By taking subsequences if necessary as $l\to\infty$, we may assume $\delta_{kl}(\theta_{i_k} -\theta_{j_k})/L(\delta(l)) \to \lambda_k$ for some nonnegative $\lambda_k$ such that $\sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k = 1$. We benefit from the fact that $f_k$ can be regarded as analytic functions on the open right half of the complex plane, and as $\delta$ tends to zero they converge uniformly on compact subsets. It follows that \begin{equation} \lim_{l\to\infty} \frac{F_{\eta(l)}(x) - F_\theta(x)}{ \alpha L(\delta(l))} = \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k f_k'(x|0), \end{equation} and the convergence is uniform on compact subsets. Let $D$ denote a finite horizontal strip within the open right half plane such that $D\cap \mathbb{R}$ encloses all possible roots $x\in (0, \infty)$ of $F_{\eta(l)}(x) - F_\theta(x)=0$ for sufficiently large $l$. This is possible from bounds on location of the crossing points (Bock et al. 1987; Roosta-Khorasani and Sz\'{e}kely, 2015). In fact, when $\delta$ is sufficiently small and $t\in (0,1)$, letting $M=\max(\theta)$ and $m=\min(\theta)$ we obtain ${\rm gamma}(n\alpha+2, m)\leq_{\rm lr} f_k(\cdot|t\delta)\leq_{\rm lr} {\rm gamma}(n\alpha +2, M)$, which implies $f_k'(x|t\delta) <0$ for $x> M/(n\alpha +1)$ and $f_k'(x|t\delta)>0$ for $x<m/(n\alpha+1)$. It follows from (\ref{eqn.inte}) that all positive real roots of $F_{\eta}(x) - F_\theta(x)=0$ must be between $m/(n\alpha+1)$ and $M/(n\alpha+1)$. We can make $D$ thin enough so that there are no other roots of $\sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k f_k'(x|0)$ within $D$ except for the unique mode of the real function $\sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k f_k(x|0)$ which, by assumption, must be a simple root. By (\ref{eqn.cross}), for large enough $l$, the number of roots of $F_{\eta(l)} - F_\theta$ within $D$, counting multiplicity, must be equal to one, which contradicts the assumption of multiple real roots.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: rescaled differences converge (as analytic functions) to a mixture derivative with a single simple root, so Hurwitz-type root counting forbids two crossings.

nodes.name: Integral representation of $F_\eta-F_\theta$
nodes.statement: F_{\eta}(x) - F_\theta(x) = \int_0^1 \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha (\theta_{i_k} - \theta_{j_k}+ 2t\delta_k) \delta_k f'_k(x|t\delta)\, {\rm d} t.
nodes.label: eqn.inte

nodes.name: Limit of rescaled cdf differences
nodes.statement: \lim_{l\to\infty} \frac{F_{\eta(l)}(x) - F_\theta(x)}{ \alpha L(\delta(l))} = \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k f_k'(x|0),
nodes.label: eqn.cross

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem.loc} is a consequence of Lemma~\ref{uni.modal} and Lemma~\ref{analytic}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 6 (unimodality of mixtures) with Lemma 5.

nodes.name: Strict unimodality of gamma-convolution mixtures
nodes.statement: In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem.loc}, let $X_i\sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha)$ and $Z_i\sim {\rm expo}(1)$ be mutually independent. Let $f_j$ denote the density of $\sum_{i=1}^n \theta_i X_i + \theta_j Z_j +\theta_k Z_k$ for $j=1,\ldots, k-1$ and that of $\sum_{i=1}^n \theta_i X_i + \theta_j Z_j +\theta_{k+1} Z_{k+1}$ for $j=k+2, \ldots, n$. Then, for any $\lambda =(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_{k-1}, \lambda_{k+2},\ldots, \lambda_n)$ such that $\lambda_i\geq 0$ and $\sum \lambda_i =1$, the mixture density $\sum_{i\neq k, k+1} \lambda_i f_i $ is unimodal with a strictly negative second derivative at the mode, and no saddle points.
assumptions: In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem.loc}, let $X_i\sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha)$ and $Z_i\sim {\rm expo}(1)$ be mutually independent.

Let $f_j$ denote the density of $\sum_{i=1}^n \theta_i X_i + \theta_j Z_j +\theta_k Z_k$ for $j=1,\ldots, k-1$ and that of $\sum_{i=1}^n \theta_i X_i + \theta_j Z_j +\theta_{k+1} Z_{k+1}$ for $j=k+2, \ldots, n$.
conclusions: Then, for any $\lambda =(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_{k-1}, \lambda_{k+2},\ldots, \lambda_n)$ such that $\lambda_i\geq 0$ and $\sum \lambda_i =1$, the mixture density $\sum_{i\neq k, k+1} \lambda_i f_i $ is unimodal with a strictly negative second derivative at the mode, and no saddle points.
nodes.statement_short: In the local configuration, every mixture of the augmented densities $f_j$ is unimodal with negative second derivative at the mode.
nodes.label: uni.modal

nodes.name: Monotonicity of derivative ratios for $X+\theta Z$
nodes.statement: For $\theta\in (0, 1)$, let $X\sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha, 1)$ and $Z\sim {\rm expo}(1)$ independently. Denote the density of $X + \theta Z$ by $h(x)$. Then (a) if $\alpha \geq 1$ then $h'(x)/g_\alpha'(x)$ strictly increases in $x\in (\alpha -1,\, \infty)$; (b) if $\alpha \geq 2$ then $h'(x)/g'_\alpha(x)$ also strictly increases in $x\in (0, \alpha -1)$; (c) if $\alpha \geq 1$ then $h'(x)/g_{\alpha +1}'(x)$ strictly decreases in each of $x\in (0, \alpha)$ and $x\in (\alpha, \infty)$; (d) parts (a)--(c) still hold when the distribution of $Z$ is replaced by a mixture of exponentials with rates $> 1$.
assumptions: For $\theta\in (0, 1)$, let $X\sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha, 1)$ and $Z\sim {\rm expo}(1)$ independently. Denote the density of $X + \theta Z$ by $h(x)$.
conclusions: (a) if $\alpha \geq 1$ then $h'(x)/g_\alpha'(x)$ strictly increases in $x\in (\alpha -1,\, \infty)$; (b) if $\alpha \geq 2$ then $h'(x)/g'_\alpha(x)$ also strictly increases in $x\in (0, \alpha -1)$; (c) if $\alpha \geq 1$ then $h'(x)/g_{\alpha +1}'(x)$ strictly decreases in each of $x\in (0, \alpha)$ and $x\in (\alpha, \infty)$;
(b) if $\alpha \geq 2$ then $h'(x)/g'_\alpha(x)$ also strictly increases in $x\in (0, \alpha -1)$;
(c) if $\alpha \geq 1$ then $h'(x)/g_{\alpha +1}'(x)$ strictly decreases in each of $x\in (0, \alpha)$ and $x\in (\alpha, \infty)$;
(d) parts (a)--(c) still hold when the distribution of $Z$ is replaced by a mixture of exponentials with rates $> 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Ratios $h'/g_\alpha'$ and $h'/g_{\alpha+1}'$ for the density of gamma plus scaled exponential are monotone on the relevant intervals.
nodes.label: lem.initial

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement: In the $\alpha=1$ case the densities are amenable to direct calculations. Let us assume $\alpha>1$. Denote $g\equiv g_\alpha$. We have \begin{equation} \theta h'(x) + h(x) = g(x),\quad x>0, \end{equation} which can be verified by comparing the Laplace transform of both sides. To prove (a), we will show $h''(x) g'(x) > h'(x) g''(x) $ for $x> \alpha -1$. Differentiating (\ref{eqn.lap}) to eliminate $h''(x)$, and noting that $\theta g''(x) +g'(x)<0$ for $x>\alpha -1$, we equivalently need to show \begin{equation} u(x)\equiv e^{x/\theta} \left[\frac{g'^2(x)}{\theta g''(x) +g'(x)}-h'(x)\right] <0,\quad x>\alpha-1. \end{equation} This holds for $x=\alpha -1$ because $g'(\alpha -1)=0$ and $h$ dominates $g$ in the likelihood ratio order. By direct calculation, we have \begin{equation} u'(x) = \frac{\theta e^{x/\theta} g'(x)(g''^2(x) - g'(x) g'''(x))}{(\theta g''(x) +g'(x))^2} <0,\quad x>\alpha -1. \end{equation} Thus $u(x)<0$ for all $x>\alpha -1$, as required. To prove (b) we only need to show that $u(x)>0$ for $x\in (0, x_*)$ and $u(x)<0$ for $x\in (x_*, \alpha -1)$ where $x_*<\alpha -1 $ is the unique positive root of $\theta g''(x) +g'(x)=0$. When $\alpha \geq 2$ we have $u(x)\to 0$ as $x\downarrow 0$ and $u'(x)>0$ for $x\in (0, x_*)\cup (x_*, \alpha -1)$. We obtain the desired sign pattern of $u$ as a consequence. To prove (c) we similarly will show $h''(x)g'_{\alpha+1}(x) < h'(x) g''_{\alpha+1}(x)$ for $x>0$. This is equivalent to $\tilde{u}(x)<0$ for $x\in (0, x^*)$ and $\tilde{u}(x)>0$ for $x\in (x^*, \infty)$, where $x^*\in (\alpha -1, \alpha)$ is the unique positive root of $\theta g''_{\alpha+1}(x) +g'_{\alpha+1}(x)=0$ and $$\tilde{u}(x)\equiv e^{x/\theta} \left[\frac{g'(x)g'_{\alpha+1}(x)}{\theta g''_{\alpha+1}(x) +g'_{\alpha+1}(x)}-h'(x)\right].$$ This sign pattern can be proved by arguments parallel to the previous parts. Part (d) is obvious.
nodes.statement_short: Use the ODE $\theta h'+h=g$ to reduce each monotonicity claim to the sign of an auxiliary function $u$, controlled through $u'$.

nodes.name: ODE linking $h$ and $g$
nodes.statement: \theta h'(x) + h(x) = g(x),\quad x>0,
nodes.label: eqn.lap

nodes.name: Auxiliary function $u$
nodes.statement: u(x)\equiv e^{x/\theta} \left[\frac{g'^2(x)}{\theta g''(x) +g'(x)}-h'(x)\right] <0,\quad x>\alpha-1.
nodes.label: eqn.u1

nodes.name: Derivative of $u$
nodes.statement: u'(x) = \frac{\theta e^{x/\theta} g'(x)(g''^2(x) - g'(x) g'''(x))}{(\theta g''(x) +g'(x))^2} <0,\quad x>\alpha -1.
nodes.label: eqn.u2

nodes.name: Supplemented likelihood ratio order
nodes.statement: Suppose $f$ and $g$ are twice continuously differentiable densities supported on an interval $I\subset (0, \infty)$. We say $f$ is dominated by $g$ in the {\it supplemented likelihood ratio} ordering, written as $f\leq_{\rm slr} g$, if (a) $f'(x)g(x)\leq f(x)g'(x)$ for all $x\in I$ and (b) $f'(x)/ g'(x)$ decreases in each of the sets $\{x:\ f'(x) >0\}$ and $\{x:\ g'(x) <0\}$.
differentia: (b) $f'(x)/ g'(x)$ decreases in each of the sets $\{x:\ f'(x) >0\}$ and $\{x:\ g'(x) <0\}$
nodes.statement_short: $f\le_{slr}g$ if $f\le_{lr}g$ and $f'/g'$ decreases where $f$ increases and where $g$ decreases.

nodes.name: Basic properties of the slr order
nodes.statement: (a) If $f\leq_{\rm slr}g $ and $g\leq_{\rm slr} h$ then $f\leq_{\rm slr} h$. (b) If $\alpha \geq 2$ and $\theta\in (0, 1)$, then $g_\alpha \leq_{\rm slr} g_\alpha * {\rm expo}(\theta)$ where $*$ denotes convolution. (c) Suppose $\alpha\geq 1$, and $\theta\in (0, 1)$, then $g_\alpha * {\rm expo}(\theta)\leq_{\rm slr} g_{\alpha+1}$. (d) Parts (b) and (c) still hold if ${\rm expo}(\theta)$ is replaced by a mixture of exponentials with rates $\geq 1$.
conclusions: (a) If $f\leq_{\rm slr}g $ and $g\leq_{\rm slr} h$ then $f\leq_{\rm slr} h$.
(b) If $\alpha \geq 2$ and $\theta\in (0, 1)$, then $g_\alpha \leq_{\rm slr} g_\alpha * {\rm expo}(\theta)$ where $*$ denotes convolution.
(c) Suppose $\alpha\geq 1$, and $\theta\in (0, 1)$, then $g_\alpha * {\rm expo}(\theta)\leq_{\rm slr} g_{\alpha+1}$.
(d) Parts (b) and (c) still hold if ${\rm expo}(\theta)$ is replaced by a mixture of exponentials with rates $\geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: slr is transitive, and gamma densities compare in slr with their convolutions with small exponentials.
nodes.label: slr.simple

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: Part (a) is obvious. Parts (b)--(d) are restating Lemma~\ref{lem.initial}.
nodes.statement_short: Transitivity is immediate; the rest restates Lemma 7.

nodes.name: slr order preserved under PF3 convolution
nodes.statement: Suppose $f$ and $g$ are unimodal (see Remark 3), $f\leq_{\rm slr} g$ and $h$ is Polya frequency order 3. Assume we can take the derivatives inside the absolutely convergent integrals and obtain $(f* h)' = f' * h$ and $(g* h)' = g' * h$. Then $f*h \leq_{\rm slr} g*h$.
assumptions: Suppose $f$ and $g$ are unimodal (see Remark 3), $f\leq_{\rm slr} g$ and $h$ is Polya frequency order 3.
Assume we can take the derivatives inside the absolutely convergent integrals and obtain $(f* h)' = f' * h$ and $(g* h)' = g' * h$.
conclusions: Then $f*h \leq_{\rm slr} g*h$.
nodes.statement_short: Convolving with a PF3 density preserves the supplemented likelihood ratio order between unimodal densities.
nodes.label: slr.prop

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement: Let us denote $\tilde{f} = f*h$ and $\tilde{g} = g*h$. Since $h$ is PF3, the likelihood ratio ordering is preserved, that is, $\tilde{f}\leq_{\rm lr} \tilde{g}$. Moreover, $\tilde{f}$ and $\tilde{g}$ are unimodal. Let $\lambda >0$ and consider the function $f'(x)-\lambda g'(x)$. By assumption $f'(x)/g'(x)$ decreases on each of $I_+ \equiv \{x:\ f'(x)>0\}$ and $I_-\equiv \{x:\ g'(x)<0\}$. Assume these are non-empty, otherwise the argument can be suitably modified. Note that by $f\leq_{\rm lr} g$ we have $g'(x)>0$ for $x\in I_+$ and $f'(x)<0$ for $x\in I_-$. On the set $I_0\equiv \{x:\ g'(x)\geq 0,\ f'(x)\leq 0\}$ we have $f'(x) -\lambda g'(x)\leq 0$. Overall $f'-\lambda g'$ changes signs at most twice, and the sign sequence is $+, -, +$ in the case of two changes. By the variation-diminishing properties of totally positive kernels (Karlin 1968), the same is true for $(f' -\lambda g')* h = \tilde{f}' -\lambda \tilde{g}'$. We need to show $\tilde{f}'/\tilde{g}'$ decreases on each of $\tilde{I}_+\equiv \{x:\ \tilde{f}'(x)>0\}$ and $\tilde{I}_-\equiv \{x:\ \tilde{g}'(x)<0\}$. Denote the upper end point of $\tilde{I}_+$ by $x_0$. For $0<\lambda < \tilde{f}(x_0)/\tilde{g}(x_0)$, if $\tilde{f}'(x)-\lambda \tilde{g}'(x)$ ever crosses zero from below in $x\in I_+$, then it must be nonnegative for $x\geq x_0$, in order not to violate the sign pattern of $+, -, +$. Thus $$\tilde{f}(x_0) = -\int_{x_0}^\infty \tilde{f}'(x)\, {\rm d}x \leq -\lambda \int_{x_0}^\infty \tilde{g}'(x)\, {\rm d}x = \lambda \tilde{g}(x_0)$$ which contradicts $\lambda < \tilde{f}(x_0)/\tilde{g}(x_0)$. With a small perturbation this still applies when $\lambda = \tilde{f}(x_0)/\tilde{g}(x_0)$. For $\lambda > \tilde{f}(x_0)/\tilde{g}(x_0)$, we have $\tilde{f}'(x)/ \tilde{g}'(x) < \lambda $ for $x\in I_+$ sufficiently close to $x_0$, because of the likelihood ratio ordering. In order not to violate the sign pattern, $\tilde{f}'(x)-\lambda \tilde{g}'(x)$ cannot cross zero from below in $x\in I_+$ in this case either. Because $\lambda$ is arbitrary, $\tilde{f}'(x)/\tilde{g}'(x)$ must decrease for $x\in I_+$. The case of $x\in \tilde{I}_-$ is similar.
nodes.statement_short: Variation diminishing: $f'-\lambda g'$ has sign pattern at most $+,-,+$, preserved by PF3 convolution; ruling out a crossing from below shows $\tilde f'/\tilde g'$ decreases.

nodes.name: Remark 3: restricted unimodality
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 3.} We impose a restricted form of unimodality, which is satisfied by the gamma convolutions. For the above proof to be valid, we need the set $I_0$ to be situated between $I_+$ and $I_-$. This will be satisfied if we assume the closures of $I_+$ and $I_-$ are intervals. So, an isolated saddle point is allowed, but not a flat ridge. We will note down such restrictions when needed.
nodes.statement_short: Unimodality here requires the closures of $I_+$ and $I_-$ to be intervals: isolated saddle points allowed, flat ridges not.

nodes.name: Comparison criterion for unimodality of two-density mixtures
nodes.statement: Let $f_i$ and $h_i,\ i=1,2,$ be twice continuously differentiable and unimodal densities supported on $(0, \infty)$ such that $$h_1\leq_{\rm slr} f_1\leq_{\rm lr} f_2\leq_{\rm slr} h_2.$$ Suppose the mixture density $p h_1 + (1- p) h_2$ is unimodal for all $p \in [0,1]$. Then so is $p f_1 + (1-p) f_2$, assuming $f'_1$ and $f_2'$ do not vanish simultaneously in between the modes of $f_1$ and $f_2$.
assumptions: Let $f_i$ and $h_i,\ i=1,2,$ be twice continuously differentiable and unimodal densities supported on $(0, \infty)$ such that $$h_1\leq_{\rm slr} f_1\leq_{\rm lr} f_2\leq_{\rm slr} h_2.$$
Suppose the mixture density $p h_1 + (1- p) h_2$ is unimodal for all $p \in [0,1]$.
assuming $f'_1$ and $f_2'$ do not vanish simultaneously in between the modes of $f_1$ and $f_2$.
conclusions: Then so is $p f_1 + (1-p) f_2$
nodes.statement_short: If $h_1\le_{slr}f_1\le_{lr}f_2\le_{slr}h_2$ and all mixtures of $h_1,h_2$ are unimodal, so are all mixtures of $f_1,f_2$.
nodes.label: comp.prop

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5
nodes.statement:
Let $x_*$ and $x^*$ denote the modes of $f_1$ and $f_2$ respectively. In the case of a possible plateau, $x_*$ (respectively, $x^*$) denotes the leftmost (respectively, rightmost) mode of $f_1$ (respectively, $f_2$). Obviously all modes of the mixture $p f_1 + (1-p) f_2 $ are in the interval $[x_*, x^*]$. Moreover, for each $x_0\in (x_*, x^*)$ such that $f_i'(x_0)
eq 0,\ i=1,2$, we may set $\lambda = - f_1'(x_0)/ f_2'(x_0)$ to obtain a stationary point of this mixture density. By the likelihood ratio ordering, we necessarily have $f_1'(x_0)<0<f_2'(x_0)$ and $\lambda >0$. To show that the mixture is unimodal, suppose $f_2'$ does not vanish on $(x_*, x^*)$. Then we can show that $-f_1'(x)/f_2'(x)$ increases on $(x_*, x^*)$, which is equivalent to  egin{equation} f_1''(x_0) f_2'(x_0) \leq f_2''(x_0) f_1'(x_0),\quad x_0\in (x_*, x^*). \end{equation} Condition (ef{mix.cond}) is necessary because, if the mixture is unimodal, then a stationary point can never be a local minimum, and hence $f_1''(x_0) +\lambda f_2''(x_0) \leq 0$. On the other hand, if $\lambda = - f_1'(x_0)/f_2'(x_0)$ is an increasing function of $x_0\in (x_*, x^*)$, then stationary points of the mixture corresponding to the same $\lambda$ form a connected interval, showing that the mixture is unimodal. A close inspection shows that (ef{mix.cond}) is sufficient as long as the saddle points of $f_1$ and $f_2$ on $(x_*, x^*)$ do not coincide. Applying this criterion to the mixture $ph_1 +(1-p) h_2 $ we have $$h_1''(x_0) h_2'(x_0) \leq h_2''(x_0) h_1'(x_0),\quad x_0\in (x_*, x^*).$$ which yields, as long as $f_1'(x_0)

nodes.statement_short: Mixture unimodality is equivalent to monotonicity of $-f_1'/f_2'$, i.e. condition (11); transfer this from $h_i$ to $f_i$ by slr ordering of $f''/f'$.

nodes.name: Unimodality of mixtures of two-term gamma sums
nodes.statement: Suppose $X_i\sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha)$ and $Z_i\sim {\rm expo}(1),\ i=1,2$, are mutually independent where $\alpha\geq 1$. Let $\delta_1, \delta_2 >0$. Then arbitrary mixtures of $\delta_1 X_1 + \delta_2 X_2$ and $\delta_1 (X_1 + Z_1) + \delta_2(X_2 + Z_2)$ are unimodal.
assumptions: Suppose $X_i\sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha)$ and $Z_i\sim {\rm expo}(1),\ i=1,2$, are mutually independent where $\alpha\geq 1$.
Let $\delta_1, \delta_2 >0$.
conclusions: Then arbitrary mixtures of $\delta_1 X_1 + \delta_2 X_2$ and $\delta_1 (X_1 + Z_1) + \delta_2(X_2 + Z_2)$ are unimodal.
nodes.label: lem.lc1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement: We show that when $\alpha=1$, such mixtures are log-concave. If $\alpha >1$ then we can write $\sum_{i=1}^2 \delta_i X_i = \sum_{i=1}^2 \delta_i (X_i^* + Y_i) $ where $X_i^*\sim {\rm expo}(1)$ and $Y_i \sim {\rm gamma}(\alpha -1)$ independently. We can similarly ``split off'' $\delta_1 Y_1 + \delta_2 Y_2$ from $\sum_{i=1}^2 \delta_i (X_i + Z_i)$. Because $\delta_1 Y_1 + \delta_2 Y_2$ is unimodal, the result follows from the log-concave result in the $\alpha=1$ case. Let us assume $\delta_2=1$ and $\delta\equiv \delta_1\in (0,1)$. When $\alpha=1$, the densities of $\delta X_1 + X_2$ and $\delta (X_1 +Z_1) + X_2 +Z_2$ are, respectively, $$h_1(x) = \frac{e^{-x} - e^{-x/\delta }}{1-\delta}; \quad h_2(x) = \frac{x(e^{-x}+ e^{-x/\delta})-2\delta h_1(x)}{(1-\delta)^2}.$$ For $\lambda > -2\delta$ and $\epsilon \equiv \delta^{-1} -1$ let $$q(x)\equiv x(e^{\epsilon x} + 1) +\lambda (e^{\epsilon x} - 1).$$ We only need to show that $q(x)$ is log-concave. A quick calculation yields $$e^{-\epsilon x}\left[q'^2(x) - q''(x) q(x)\right] = e^{\epsilon x} + e^{-\epsilon x} -2 - (\epsilon x)^2 + (\lambda \epsilon + 2)^2 $$ which is positive for all $x>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\alpha=1$ by splitting off a unimodal gamma part, then verify log-concavity of an explicit function $q$.

nodes.name: Strict log-concavity of exponential mixture plus exponential
nodes.statement: Let $Y$ be an arbitrary mixture of $k\geq 1$ exponentials with means $\delta_i,\ i=1,\ldots, k$ such that $\max(\delta_i)\leq \delta$. Let $Z\sim {\rm expo}(\delta)$ independently of $Y$. Then $Y+Z$ is strictly log-concave.
assumptions: Let $Y$ be an arbitrary mixture of $k\geq 1$ exponentials with means $\delta_i,\ i=1,\ldots, k$ such that $\max(\delta_i)\leq \delta$.
Let $Z\sim {\rm expo}(\delta)$ independently of $Y$.
conclusions: Then $Y+Z$ is strictly log-concave.
nodes.label: lem.lc2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement: Suppose $\max(\delta_i)<\delta$. The density of $U\equiv Y+Z$ can be written as $h(u) = \sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i (e^{-u/\delta} - e^{-u/\delta_i}) $ for some constants $\lambda_i>0$. We know $h(u)$ is strictly log-concave on $(0, \infty)$ because $e^{u/\delta} h(u)$ is strictly concave. A slight modification works when $\max(\delta_i) =\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the density explicitly and note $e^{u/\delta}h(u)$ is strictly concave.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: We shall use the notation $\leq_{\rm slr}$ with the random variables as well as the densities. Let $Y_1$ be an arbitrary mixture of $\theta_j Z_j$ for $j=1,\ldots, k-1$; let $Y_2$ be an arbitrary mixture of $\theta_j Z_j$ for $j=k+2, \ldots, n$. Then $Y_1\leq_{\rm lr} \theta_k Z_k\leq_{\rm lr} Y_2$, and these have strictly decreasing densities. Define $$\tilde{X}\equiv \theta_n X_n + \theta_{k+1} X_{k+1},\quad W_1 \equiv \tilde{X} + \theta_k Z_k + Y_1,\quad W_2 \equiv \tilde{X} +\theta_{k+1} Z_{k+1} + Y_2.$$ We have $W_1\leq_{\rm lr} W_2$, and $W_1, W_2$ are unimodal (since $\alpha\geq 1$); $W_1$ is in fact log-concave by Lemma~\ref{lem.lc2}. If we can show that arbitrary mixtures of $W_1$ and $W_2$ are unimodal, then so are those of $f_j,\ j=1,\ldots, k-1, k+2,\ldots, n,$ by adding $\sum_{i\neq k+1, n} \theta_i X_i$, which is log-concave. Lemma~\ref{lem.initial} yields $\theta_n X_n + Y_2 \leq_{\rm slr} \theta_n (X_n + Z_n)$. Convolving both sides with $\theta_{k+1} (X_{k+1} + Z_{k+1})$, which is PF3 (Karlin 1968), we obtain $$W_2\leq_{\rm slr} \theta_{k+1}(X_{k+1}+Z_{k+1})+\theta_n (X_n +Z_n).$$ Lemma~\ref{lem.initial} also yields \begin{equation} \theta_n(X_n+Z_n) \leq_{\rm slr} \theta_n(X_n+Z_n) + \theta_k Z_k \leq_{\rm slr} \theta_n(X_n+Z_n) + \theta_k Z_k + Y_1, \end{equation} where the second $\leq_{\rm slr}$ is obtained by convolving $\theta_n(X_n+Z_n) \leq_{\rm slr} \theta_n(X_n+Z_n) + Y_1$ with $\theta_k Z_k$. Convolving (\ref{slr.ineqs}) with $\theta_{k+1}(X_{k+1}+Z_{k+1})$ yields $$W_2\leq_{\rm slr} W_3\equiv \theta_{k+1}(X_{k+1}+Z_{k+1})+\theta_n (X_n +Z_n) + \theta_k Z_k + Y_1.$$ By Proposition ~\ref{comp.prop}, we only need to show that arbitrary mixtures of $W_1$ and $W_3$ are unimodal. But this is a consequence of Lemma~\ref{lem.lc1}, which shows that arbitrary mixtures of $\tilde{X}$ and $ \theta_{k+1} (X_{k+1}+Z_{k+1}) + \theta_n (X_n + Z_n)$ are unimodal, and Lemma~\ref{lem.lc2}, which shows that $\theta_k Z_k + Y_1$ is log-concave. Strict unimodality, in the sense of a strictly negative second derivative at the mode, and no saddle points, can be established by a careful examination of the above steps. For example, in Proposition~\ref{comp.prop}, the claim still holds if we use strict unimodality in both the condition on $h_i$ and the conclusion on $f_i$. Also, in addition to being unimodal, the density of a mixture of $\tilde{X}$ and $ \theta_{k+1} (X_{k+1}+Z_{k+1}) + \theta_n (X_n + Z_n)$ is analytic on $(0, \infty)$, vanishes at $0+$, and has a bounded first derivative. One can then verify that the step of adding $\theta_k Z_k +Y_1$, which is strictly log-concave, yields a strictly unimodal density.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to mixtures of $W_1$ and $W_2$, sandwich $W_2$ in slr order via Lemma 7 and PF3 convolution, then apply Proposition 5 with Lemmas 8 and 9.

nodes.name: Chain of slr inequalities
nodes.statement: \theta_n(X_n+Z_n) \leq_{\rm slr} \theta_n(X_n+Z_n) + \theta_k Z_k \leq_{\rm slr} \theta_n(X_n+Z_n) + \theta_k Z_k + Y_1,
nodes.label: slr.ineqs

nodes.name: Verify Theorem 1's conditions for n=3
nodes.statement: When $n=3$, conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm1} can be written as $\eta_{(1)} > \theta_{(1)},\ \eta_{(3)} < \theta_{(3)}$ and $\theta_1\theta_2\theta_3 <\eta_1\eta_2\eta_3$. It is easy to verify that if $\eta\prec \theta$ then these conditions are satisfied (if any $\eta_i=\theta_j$ then the problem reduces to the $n=2$ case).
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the conditions of Theorem 1 for $n=3$ and check majorization implies them

nodes.name: Extend to n>=3
nodes.statement: As noted by Diaconis and Perlman, when $\alpha\geq 1$, one may extend the validity of the UCC for $n=3$ to $n\geq 3$ provided that the weight vectors differ in at most three components.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to $n\ge3$ by Diaconis-Perlman's observation

nodes.name: Necessity
nodes.statement: {\bf Necessity.} Suppose $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once from below. Then $F_\eta(x) -F_\theta(x)$ is negative for sufficiently small $x>0$ and is positive for sufficiently large $x$. But $$\frac{1 - F_\theta(x)}{1 - F_\eta(x)} \leq \frac{\Pr(\theta_2 (X_1+X_2) > x)}{\Pr(\eta_2 X_2 > x)}.$$ The latter ratio is asymptotic to $g_{2\alpha}(x/\theta_2)/ g_\alpha(x/\eta_2)$ as $x\to \infty$ where $g_\alpha(t) \equiv t^{\alpha -1} e^{-t} /\Gamma(\alpha)$. It is clear that if $\theta_2 < \eta_2$ then $(1 - F_\theta(x))/(1 - F_\eta(x))\to 0$ as $x\to\infty$ and hence we must have $\theta_2> \eta_2$. (It is easy to dismiss the boundary case $\theta_2 = \eta_2$.) On the other hand, $$\lim_{x\downarrow 0} \frac{F_\theta(x)}{F_\eta(x)} = \lim_{x\downarrow 0} \frac{ f_\theta(x) }{f_\eta(x)} = \left(\frac{\theta_1\theta_2}{\eta_1\eta_2}\right)^{-\alpha},$$ see, for example, Yu (2009), Equation (13). Hence we must have $\theta_1\theta_2 \leq \eta_1\eta_2$. To rule out the boundary case, note that if $\theta_1\theta_2 = \eta_1\eta_2$, then $(\log\eta_1, \log\eta_2)\prec (\log \theta_1, \log \theta_2)$ and, by Lemma~\ref{lem1}, there is no crossing.
nodes.statement_short: Derive the two conditions from a single crossing

nodes.name: Crossing pattern at the ends
nodes.statement: {\bf Necessity.} Suppose $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once from below. Then $F_\eta(x) -F_\theta(x)$ is negative for sufficiently small $x>0$ and is positive for sufficiently large $x$.
nodes.statement_short: A single crossing from below fixes signs near $0$ and $\infty$

nodes.name: Tail comparison
nodes.statement: But $$\frac{1 - F_\theta(x)}{1 - F_\eta(x)} \leq \frac{\Pr(\theta_2 (X_1+X_2) > x)}{\Pr(\eta_2 X_2 > x)}.$$ The latter ratio is asymptotic to $g_{2\alpha}(x/\theta_2)/ g_\alpha(x/\eta_2)$ as $x\to \infty$ where $g_\alpha(t) \equiv t^{\alpha -1} e^{-t} /\Gamma(\alpha)$. It is clear that if $\theta_2 < \eta_2$ then $(1 - F_\theta(x))/(1 - F_\eta(x))\to 0$ as $x\to\infty$ and hence we must have $\theta_2> \eta_2$. (It is easy to dismiss the boundary case $\theta_2 = \eta_2$.)
nodes.statement_short: Tail asymptotics force $\theta_2>\eta_2$

nodes.name: Small-x ratio
nodes.statement: On the other hand, $$\lim_{x\downarrow 0} \frac{F_\theta(x)}{F_\eta(x)} = \lim_{x\downarrow 0} \frac{ f_\theta(x) }{f_\eta(x)} = \left(\frac{\theta_1\theta_2}{\eta_1\eta_2}\right)^{-\alpha},$$ see, for example, Yu (2009), Equation (13). Hence we must have $\theta_1\theta_2 \leq \eta_1\eta_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Small-$x$ density ratio forces $\theta_1\theta_2\le\eta_1\eta_2$

nodes.name: Boundary case via Lemma 1
nodes.statement: To rule out the boundary case, note that if $\theta_1\theta_2 = \eta_1\eta_2$, then $(\log\eta_1, \log\eta_2)\prec (\log \theta_1, \log \theta_2)$ and, by Lemma~\ref{lem1}, there is no crossing.
nodes.statement_short: Equality of products gives log-majorization, so no crossing by Lemma 1

nodes.name: Sufficiency
nodes.statement: {\bf Sufficiency.} Assume $\theta_1\theta_2 < \eta_1 \eta_2$ and $\theta_2 > \eta_2$. Retracing the proof of the necessity part, we can deduce that $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ at least once, from below. To show that the crossing point is unique we slightly extend the arguments of Diaconis and Perlman (1990). We have $$F_\theta(x) - F_\eta(x) = x u^{-2} \int_0^\infty (H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u)) g_{2\alpha}(x/u) {\rm d} u$$ where $H_\theta(u) = \Pr(\theta_1 W_1 + \theta_2 W_2 \leq u)$ and $W_1$ is a beta($\alpha, \alpha$) random variable with $W_1 = 1-W_2 = X_1/(X_1 + X_2).$ The kernel $g_{2\alpha}(x/u)$ is strictly totally positive (STP) for $(x, u) \in (0, \infty)^2$. The claim would follow from variation-diminishing properties of STP kernels if we can show that $H_\theta(u) -H_\eta(u)$ changes signs only once, from $+$ to $-$, as u increases on $(0, \infty)$. Note that $$H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u) =B\left(\frac{\eta_2 - u}{\eta_2 -\eta_1}\right) - B\left(\frac{\theta_2 -u}{\theta_2 -\theta_1}\right)$$ where $B(\cdot)$ denotes the beta($\alpha, \alpha$) distribution function. Let $$u^* = \frac{\theta_2 \eta_1 - \eta_2 \theta_1}{\theta_2 -\theta_1 -\eta_2 +\eta_1}.$$ Under the assumptions we have $\theta_1< \eta_1 \leq \eta_2 <\theta_2$. It follows that $\eta_1 \leq u^* \leq \eta_2 $ and $$ H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u) \begin{cases} > 0 & {\rm if}\ \theta_1 < u < u^*,\\ < 0 & {\rm if}\ u^* < u < \theta_2,\\ =0 & {\rm otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ That is, $H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u)$ has only one sign change at $u^*$, as needed.
nodes.statement_short: Show the conditions give exactly one crossing

nodes.name: At least one crossing
nodes.statement: {\bf Sufficiency.} Assume $\theta_1\theta_2 < \eta_1 \eta_2$ and $\theta_2 > \eta_2$. Retracing the proof of the necessity part, we can deduce that $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ at least once, from below.
nodes.statement_short: Retrace necessity to get at least one crossing from below

nodes.name: Mixture representation with STP kernel
nodes.statement: To show that the crossing point is unique we slightly extend the arguments of Diaconis and Perlman (1990). We have $$F_\theta(x) - F_\eta(x) = x u^{-2} \int_0^\infty (H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u)) g_{2\alpha}(x/u) {\rm d} u$$ where $H_\theta(u) = \Pr(\theta_1 W_1 + \theta_2 W_2 \leq u)$ and $W_1$ is a beta($\alpha, \alpha$) random variable with $W_1 = 1-W_2 = X_1/(X_1 + X_2).$ The kernel $g_{2\alpha}(x/u)$ is strictly totally positive (STP) for $(x, u) \in (0, \infty)^2$. The claim would follow from variation-diminishing properties of STP kernels if we can show that $H_\theta(u) -H_\eta(u)$ changes signs only once, from $+$ to $-$, as u increases on $(0, \infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $F_\theta-F_\eta$ as an STP-kernel transform of $H_\theta-H_\eta$; reduce to one sign change

nodes.name: Beta representation and u*
nodes.statement: Note that $$H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u) =B\left(\frac{\eta_2 - u}{\eta_2 -\eta_1}\right) - B\left(\frac{\theta_2 -u}{\theta_2 -\theta_1}\right)$$ where $B(\cdot)$ denotes the beta($\alpha, \alpha$) distribution function. Let $$u^* = \frac{\theta_2 \eta_1 - \eta_2 \theta_1}{\theta_2 -\theta_1 -\eta_2 +\eta_1}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Express $H_\theta-H_\eta$ via the beta cdf and define $u^*$

nodes.name: Single sign change at u*
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions we have $\theta_1< \eta_1 \leq \eta_2 <\theta_2$. It follows that $\eta_1 \leq u^* \leq \eta_2 $ and $$ H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u) \begin{cases} > 0 & {\rm if}\ \theta_1 < u < u^*,\\ < 0 & {\rm if}\ u^* < u < \theta_2,\\ =0 & {\rm otherwise}. \end{cases} $$ That is, $H_\theta(u) - H_\eta(u)$ has only one sign change at $u^*$, as needed.
nodes.statement_short: Show $H_\theta-H_\eta$ changes sign only at $u^*$

nodes.name: Base case n=2
nodes.statement: We use induction on $n$. The case of $n=2$ is given by Proposition~\ref{prop1}.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$; base case from Proposition 1

nodes.name: Inductive step setup
nodes.statement: Suppose $n\geq 3$. The following argument works for $k<n$, and can be modified (with a different definition of $\tau$) to handle the $k=n$ case.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step for $n\ge3$, treating $k<n$

nodes.name: Intermediate vector tau
nodes.statement: Let us consider $\tau \equiv (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_{k-2}, \delta, \eta_{k}, \theta_{k+1}, \ldots, \theta_n),$ where $$\delta_*\equiv \frac{\theta_{k-1}\theta_{k}}{\eta_{k}}\leq \delta\leq \min\left(\theta_{k},\, \prod_{i\neq k} \eta_i/\prod_{i\neq k-1, k} \theta_i\right)\equiv \delta^*.$$ It is easy to see that $\delta_*<\delta^*$, and for $\delta\in (\delta_*, \delta^*)$ we have $\delta > \theta_{k-1}$ and $\prod_{i=1}^n \eta_i > \prod_{i=1}^n \tau_i > \prod_{i=1}^n \theta_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\tau(\delta)$ interpolating between $\theta$ and $\eta$

nodes.name: One sign change for tau-eta
nodes.statement: Also, $\tau_i <\eta_i$ for $i< k-1$ and $\tau_i >\eta_i$ for $i\geq k+1$ (including $i=n$ since $k<n$). Hence the sequence $\tau_{(i)} - \eta_i,\ i=1,\ldots, n$, has exactly one sign change, whether $\delta > \eta_{k-1}$ or not. (In the special case $k=2$ we have $\delta < \eta_1$.) Here we use $\tau_{(i)}$ rather than $\tau_i$ to account for possible switching between $\eta_{k-1}$ and $\delta$ when we rearrange $\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: Check $\tau_{(i)}-\eta_i$ has one sign change

nodes.name: Apply induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: As $\tau$ and $\theta$ differ in only two components, and $\tau$ and $\eta$ have at least one ($\eta_k$) in common, by the induction hypothesis, $F_\tau$ crosses $F_\theta$ at most once, from below (say at $x_*$) and $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\tau$ at most once, from below (say at $x^*$).
nodes.statement_short: Induction hypothesis gives at most one crossing for each pair

nodes.name: Annihilation of crossings
nodes.statement: When $\alpha \geq 1$ the gamma density is log-concave, which ensures that adding identical components does not create multiple crossings. It is possible that the original single crossing is annihilated. If $\delta$ is large then $F_\tau$ could stay entirely below $F_\theta$ (effectively $x_*=\infty$). It is not possible, however, for $F_\eta$ to stay entirely below $F_\tau$, because $\tau_n>\eta_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Log-concavity prevents extra crossings; discuss when crossings vanish

nodes.name: Monotonicity of crossing points
nodes.statement: Note that $F_\tau$ stochastically increases in $\delta$, which implies that $x_*$ increases while $x^*$ decreases in $\delta$. This monotonicity can then be used to show that the crossing points (as long as they are finite) are continuous functions of $\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Crossing points are monotone in $\delta$

nodes.name: Continuity of crossing points
nodes.statement: Specifically, fix $\delta_0\in (\delta_*, \delta^*)$ such that $x_*(\delta_0)$ is finite. Then, by the continuity of $F_\theta$ and $F_\tau$, and the monotonicity of $x_*$, we have $$F_\theta(x_*(\delta_0 +)) = \lim_{\delta \downarrow \delta_0} F_\theta(x_*(\delta)) = \lim_{\delta \downarrow \delta_0} F_\tau (x_*(\delta)) = F_{\tau(\delta_0)}(x_*(\delta_0 + )). $$ That is, $F_\theta$ and $F_{\tau(\delta_0)}$ crosses at $x_*(\delta_0 +)$. By uniqueness of the crossing point we have $x_*(\delta_0) = x_*(\delta_0 +)$, and similarly $x_*(\delta_0) = x_*(\delta_0 -)$, showing that $x_*$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Prove continuity of $x_*$ in $\delta$

nodes.name: Endpoint delta_*
nodes.statement: At $\delta = \delta_*$, we have $F_\tau\leq_{\rm st} F_\theta$ by Lemma~\ref{lem1}. So there is no crossing between $F_\tau$ and $F_\theta$. That is, $x_*\downarrow 0$ as $\delta\downarrow \delta_*$ and $\lim_{\delta\downarrow \delta_*} x^* >0$.
nodes.statement_short: At $\delta_*$, Lemma 1 gives no crossing, so $x_*\to0$

nodes.name: Endpoint theta_k
nodes.statement: At $\delta = \theta_k$ we have $F_\tau\geq_{\rm st} F_\theta$. Thus $x_*\uparrow \infty$ as $\delta\uparrow \theta_k$ if $\delta^*=\theta_k$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\delta^*=\theta_k$ then $x_*\to\infty$

nodes.name: Endpoint delta^*
nodes.statement: The other possibility is $\delta^* = \prod_{i\neq k} \eta_i/\prod_{i\neq k, k-1} \theta_i$. In this case, at $\delta=\delta^*$ we have $F_\tau\geq_{\rm st} F_\eta$ again by Lemma~\ref{lem1}, because $\log\eta\prec \log\tau$. Indeed, because $\log(\eta_i/\tau_i)$ changes signs only once (after $\tau$ is arranged in increasing order), $\sum_{i=1}^l \log(\eta_i/\tau_i)$ first increases, and then decreases. At $l=1$ we have $\eta_1>\tau_1$. At $l=n$ we have $\sum_{i=1}^n \log(\eta_i/ \tau_i) = 0$. Thus $\sum_{i=1}^l \log(\eta_i/ \tau_i) \geq 0$ for all $l=1,\ldots, n$, that is, $\log\eta\prec\log\tau$. It follows that $x^*\downarrow 0$ as $\delta\uparrow \delta^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise log-majorization and Lemma 1 give $x^*\to0$

nodes.name: Intermediate value conclusion
nodes.statement: Regardless of whether $\delta^*=\theta_k$, we have $x_*< x^*$ as $\delta\to \delta_*$ and $x_* > x^*$ as $\delta\to \delta^*$. By continuity, there exists some $\delta$ such that $x_*=x^*$ and \begin{align*} F_\theta(x) &> F_\tau(x)> F_\eta(x),\quad 0<x<x^*;\\ F_\theta(x) &< F_\tau(x)< F_\eta(x),\quad x^*<x<\infty. \end{align*} It follows that $F_\eta$ crosses $F_\theta$ exactly once, from below.
nodes.statement_short: By continuity choose $\delta$ with $x_*=x^*$ and conclude one crossing

nodes.name: Stationary point construction
nodes.statement: For any $x_0\in (0, \alpha)$ one may set $\lambda \equiv \lambda(x_0)= - g'_{\alpha}(x_0) / g'_{1+\alpha}(x_0)$ and obtain a function $s(x)\equiv \lambda g_{1+\alpha}(x) + g_{\alpha}(x)$ such that $s'(x_0) = 0$. Note that since $x_0$ is between the modes of $g_{1+\alpha}$ and $g_{\alpha}$ we necessarily have $\lambda>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\lambda(x_0)$ making $x_0$ a stationary point of $s$

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: We show that $\alpha\in (0, 1)$ is equivalent to the existence of some $x_0$ such that $s''(x_0)>0$, which indicates a local minimum.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the existence of $x_0$ with $s''(x_0)>0$

nodes.name: Compute s''
nodes.statement: By direct calculation we get $$s''(x_0) = \lambda g''_{1+\alpha}(x_0) + g''_{\alpha}(x_0) = -\lambda'(x_0) g'_{1+\alpha}(x_0)$$ with $$ \lambda'(x_0) =\frac{\alpha (x_0^2 + 2(1-\alpha )x_0 - \alpha(1-\alpha))}{(\alpha x_0- x_0^2)^2}. $$ Thus $s''(x_0)$ has the opposite sign of $x_0^2 + 2(1-\alpha )x_0 - \alpha(1-\alpha)$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $s''(x_0)$ via $\lambda'(x_0)$; its sign is that of a quadratic

nodes.name: Sign of quadratic
nodes.statement: If $\alpha<1$ then this quadratic is negative for sufficiently small $x_0>0$; if $\alpha \geq 1$ then it is positive for all $x_0>0$. Thus a local minimum exists if and only if $\alpha\in (0, 1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Quadratic negative near $0$ iff $\alpha<1$, concluding

nodes.name: Bimodal mixture
nodes.statement: Since $\alpha\in (0, 1)$, by Lemma~\ref{lem3} one can choose $\lambda>0$ such that $s(x)\equiv \lambda g_{1+\alpha}(x) + g_{\alpha}(x)$ is bimodal, with a local minimum at $x_0>0$. Choose $w>0$ small enough so that $s'(x_0 -w)<0$ and $s'(x_0+w)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3 gives a bimodal mixture with a local minimum at $x_0$

nodes.name: Construct theta and auxiliary sums
nodes.statement: Let $\theta_1 = \epsilon-\delta,\, \theta_2 = \epsilon + \delta -\lambda\delta^2,\, \theta_3 = 1+\epsilon + \lambda\delta^2$, where $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ are to be determined. We require $\epsilon>\delta>0$ and $\epsilon < 1/\lambda$ so that the weight vector $\theta$ is positive. Let $X_i,\, i=1,2,\ldots$ be independent gamma($\alpha, 1$) variates and $Z_i\sim {\rm expo}(1)$ independently. Define $G_0\equiv \sum_{i=1}^3 \theta_iX_i$. Denote the density of $G_1\equiv G_0 + \sum_{i=1}^2\theta_iZ_i$ by $f_1$ and that of $G_2\equiv G_0+\sum_{i=2}^3 \theta_i Z_i$ by $f_2$.

nodes.name: Derivative via Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Let $s'_\delta(x) \equiv \lambda (1 -\delta +2\lambda\delta^2) f'_2(x) + (1-\lambda\delta/2) f'_1(x)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem2} and the chain rule, with $F_\theta(x) =\Pr(G_0\leq x)$, we have $$\frac{\partial}{\partial \delta}F_\theta(x) = 2\alpha\delta s'_\delta(x).$$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2 and chain rule express $\partial_\delta F_\theta$ through $s'_\delta$

nodes.name: Choose epsilon
nodes.statement: Since $s'_\delta(x) \to s'(x)$ as $\epsilon\downarrow 0$, we may choose $\epsilon<1/\lambda$ small enough so that, as long as $\delta <\epsilon$, we have $s'_\delta(x_0-w)<0$ and $s'_\delta(x_0+w)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\epsilon$ so $s'_\delta$ keeps the sign pattern near $x_0$

nodes.name: Mean value theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\eta = (\epsilon, \epsilon, 1+\epsilon)$. Then $\eta\prec \theta$ and by the mean value theorem $$F_\theta(x) - F_\eta(x) = 2\alpha \delta\delta^*s'_{\delta^*}(x),\quad \delta^*\in (0, \delta).$$
nodes.statement_short: Set $\eta$ and apply the mean value theorem

nodes.name: Count sign changes
nodes.statement: But the right hand side is strictly negative at $x = x_0-w$ and strictly positive at $x = x_0+w$, indicating at least one sign change in $x\in (x_0 - w, x_0 + w)$. Since $F_\theta(x) - F_\eta(x)>0$ for sufficiently small $x>0$ and $F_\theta(x) - F_\eta(x)<0$ for sufficiently large $x$, we have at least two additional sign changes, both from $+$ to $-$, in $x\in (0, x_0 - w]$ and $x\in [x_0+w, \infty)$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Wrong-direction crossing plus boundary behaviour gives three sign changes

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Assume the coordinates of $\theta$ (respectively, $\eta$) are arranged in increasing order, and assume $\theta\neq \eta$. Let $\tilde{\theta}$ (also arranged in increasing order) be such that $\eta\prec \tilde{\theta}$ and (\ref{major.V}) is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Order coordinates and fix $\tilde\theta$

nodes.name: Part (a)
nodes.statement: Part (a). Note that $\tilde{\theta}_i \geq \theta_i$ for $1\leq i<k_2$. From $\eta\prec\tilde{\theta}$ we get $\log\eta\prec^w \log\tilde{\theta}$ and $$\prod_{i=1}^l \eta_i \geq \prod_{i=1}^l \tilde{\theta}_i \geq \prod_{i=1}^l \theta_i,\quad 1\leq l<k_2. $$ For $i\geq k_2$ we have $\eta_i \leq \theta_i$ which means $\prod_{i=1}^l (\eta_i /\theta_i)$ between $l=k_2-1$ and $l=n$ is minimized at $l=n$. Thus, to ensure $\log \eta \prec^w \log \theta$ we only need $\prod_{i=1}^n \eta_i \geq \prod_{i=1}^n \theta_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare partial products to get weak log-majorization

nodes.name: Part (b)
nodes.statement: Part (b). We may define $$\theta^*_i \equiv \begin{cases} \theta_i & i< k_2, \\ \theta_i^{1-\lambda} \eta_i^{\lambda} & i\geq k_2; \end{cases} \quad \quad \lambda = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \log (\theta_i/\eta_i) }{\sum_{i=k_2}^n \log (\theta_i / \eta_i)}.$$ Then $\lambda\in [0, 1],\, \theta^*\leq \theta$ (coordinate-wise), and $\prod_{i=1}^n (\eta_i/\theta^*_i) = 1$. The reasoning of part (a) yields $\log\eta \prec \log \theta^*$. By Lemma~\ref{lem1}, $F_\eta\leq_{\rm st} F_{\theta^*}\leq_{\rm st} F_\theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Shrink top coordinates to equalize products, then apply Lemma 1

nodes.name: Base case n=3
nodes.statement: We will use induction on $n$. The case of $n=3$ is covered by Theorem~\ref{thm1}.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$; base case from Theorem 1

nodes.name: Indices j and k
nodes.statement: For $n\geq 4$ assume $\theta_1\leq \cdots\leq \theta_n,\ \eta_1\leq\cdots\leq \eta_n$, and $\theta_i\neq \eta_i$ for all $i$. Let us define $$j \equiv \min\{i:\ \theta_i > \eta_i,\, 1\leq i\leq n\};\quad k \equiv \max\{i:\ \theta_i < \eta_i,\, 1\leq i\leq n\}.$$ These indices must exist because $\theta_n>\eta_n$ and $\theta_1<\eta_1$. Moreover, we have $j \geq 2,\ k\leq n-1,\ j\neq k$ and $k\geq j-1$. Consider two cases:
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: define the sign-change indices $j,k$

nodes.name: Case (a)
nodes.statement: (a) $k=j-1$. Then $\log(\eta_i/\theta_i)$ has only one sign change and the claim follows from Theorem~\ref{thm1}.
nodes.statement_short: One sign change: Theorem 1 applies

nodes.name: Case (b)
nodes.statement_short: Two-parameter interpolation argument

nodes.name: Construct tau(t)
nodes.statement: (b) $k > j$. Since $\eta \prec_{\rm V} \theta$, there exists $\tilde{\theta}$ such that $\eta\prec \tilde{\theta}$ and (\ref{major.V}) holds. In (\ref{major.V}) we necessarily have $k_1\leq j-1$ and $k_2\geq k+1$, and hence $\tilde{\theta}_i =\theta_i,\ i=j, \ldots, k.$ Let $\delta= \eta -\tilde{\theta}$. Then $\delta_i\geq 0$ for $i<j$ and $\delta_i \leq 0$ for $i>k$. Define a weight vector $\tau $ parameterized by $t_1, t_2$ as follows. \begin{equation} \tau_i \equiv \begin{cases} \theta_i + t_1 \delta_i & i< j,\\ \theta_i - t_1 \sum_{l=1}^{j-1} \delta_l & i=j,\\ \theta_i & j<i<k;\\ \theta_i - t_2 \sum_{l=k+1}^n \delta_l & i=k,\\ \theta_i + t_2 \delta_i & i> k. \end{cases} \end{equation} We require $0\leq t_1\leq c_1$ and $0\leq t_2\leq c_2$ where $$c_1 = \frac{\theta_j - \eta_j}{\sum_{i=1}^{j-1} \delta_i};\quad c_2 = \frac{\theta_k - \eta_k}{\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} \delta_i}.$$ Because $\eta\prec\tilde{\theta}$, we have $\sum_{i=1}^{j-1} \delta_i \geq -\delta_j > 0,\ \sum_{i=k+1}^{n} \delta_i \leq -\delta_k <0$ and $c_1, c_2\in (0, 1)$. Define $\tilde{\tau} = \tau + \tilde{\theta} - \theta$. Using $t_i\leq c_i,\ i=1,2$, we can show that components of $\tilde{\tau}$ are in increasing order, and that $\eta\prec \tilde{\tau}$. Moreover, $\tau_i\leq \tilde{\tau}_i \leq \eta_i$ for $i<j$ and $\tau_i\geq \tilde{\tau}_i \geq \eta_i$ for $i>k$. It follows that $\eta\prec_{\rm V} \tau$. Also, from (\ref{tau.def}) and (i) $\tau_i\leq \eta_i \leq \eta_j\leq \tau_j$ for $i<j$ and (ii) $\tau_i\geq \eta_i \geq \eta_k\geq \tau_k$ for $i>k$, we can deduce that $\tau\prec \theta$, which yields $\prod_{i=1}^n (\tau_i/\theta_i)\geq 1$. In fact, if we have $t,\, \tilde{t}$ such that $0\leq t_i\leq \tilde{t}_i\leq c_i,\ i=1,2$, then $\eta\prec_{\rm V} \tau(\tilde{t})\prec \tau(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\tau(t_1,t_2)$ and check V-majorization properties
